introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL 2 questions in this section. Section C: answer 2 questions out of 3; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first two will be considered. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; $0^\circ$C = 273 K.

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the equipment labelled **A** and **B**. A: ......... B: ......... *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown: **A** is a **conical flask** (Erlenmeyer flask); **B** is a **burette**, held vertically in a clamp on a retort stand.

questions.enonce_markdown: In which of the apparatus is the indicator usually put during titration? *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: In the **conical flask (A)**, together with the solution of known volume taken with the pipette. The indicator is not put in the burette.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why is it always advisable to put the NaOH in apparatus **A** and not in **B**? *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali that **attacks glass**: in the burette it can make the glass tap stick or jam and corrode the burette. In the flask, the colour change is also easier to see and no part of the equipment can be damaged.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In one of such experiments, the student used 25 cm$^3$ of 0.2 M NaOH solution, dilute hydrochloric acid and phenolphthalein indicator.

(i) Briefly describe the procedure for the titration. *[4 marks]*

(ii) State the colour change at the end point. Initial colour: ......... Final colour: ......... *[2 marks]*

(iii) If the volume of the dilute hydrochloric acid at the end point was 15 cm$^3$, calculate the concentration of the dilute hydrochloric acid.

$\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Rinse the pipette with the NaOH solution and use it to transfer **25.0 cm$^3$ of 0.2 M NaOH** into a clean conical flask. Add 2-3 drops of **phenolphthalein** (the solution turns pink). Rinse the burette with the dilute HCl, fill it and record the **initial reading**. Run the acid from the burette into the flask a little at a time, **swirling the flask**, and go drop by drop near the end until the pink colour **just disappears**. Record the **final reading**; the volume of acid used is final minus initial. Repeat until two (concordant) results agree.

(ii) **Initial colour:** pink. **Final colour:** colourless.

(iii) Moles of NaOH: $n = c \times V = 0.2 \times \dfrac{25}{1000} = 0.005\ \mathrm{mol}$.

From the equation, $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ react in the ratio 1 : 1, so $n(\mathrm{HCl}) = 0.005\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Concentration of the acid: $c = \dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{0.005}{15/1000} = 0.333\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, that is about **0.33 M**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In order to prepare and collect a dry sample of carbon dioxide, a student was provided with the following: a thistle funnel, 2 flat-bottomed flasks, a gas jar, delivery tubes, rubber bungs, solid calcium carbonate, dilute hydrochloric acid, concentrated sulphuric acid.

(i) State one observation made when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a lump of calcium carbonate in a test tube. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Draw the experimental set up you would use to prepare the gas. *[4 marks]*

(iii) Identify a reagent the student would use to prove that the gas is carbon dioxide and state the observation. Reagent: ......... Observation: ......... *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Effervescence (fizzing)**: bubbles of a colourless gas are given off and the calcium carbonate gradually dissolves. $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)}$

(ii) *What to draw (in order, left to right):*

1. **Flask 1** (generator): flat-bottomed flask containing lumps of **solid calcium carbonate**, closed by a rubber bung through which pass a **thistle funnel** (its lower end dipping **below the acid**, which is added through it as **dilute hydrochloric acid**) and a delivery tube.
2. **Flask 2** (drying flask): flat-bottomed flask containing **concentrated sulphuric acid** to dry the gas. The delivery tube from flask 1 dips **below the surface of the acid**; a second, short delivery tube leaves from above the acid.
3. A **gas jar** to collect the gas by **upward delivery (downward displacement of air)**: the delivery tube reaches the bottom of the jar, because carbon dioxide is **denser than air**.

Label: thistle funnel, dilute HCl, calcium carbonate, conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ (drying agent), gas jar, carbon dioxide.

(iii) **Reagent:** **lime water** (calcium hydroxide solution). **Observation:** the lime water turns **milky (cloudy)** as a white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following experimental setup was used by a student to test the electrical conductivity of two liquids **A** and **B**.

![fig-2](gce-ol-chemistry-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_2.png)

(i) Liquids **A** and **B** are kerosene and water. State the observation at the level of the bulb for liquid **B**. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: **The bulb does not light** (no current flows). Kerosene and pure water are covalent substances with practically no free ions, so neither can carry the current. (If tap water were used, the bulb would at most glow very dimly.)
